findings.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:165 — [P1/100] `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);`: the database insert has already committed before this fallible external-calendar call, so a provider failure leaves durable attendees absent from the calendar and a retry rejects them as already present instead of repairing the partial state.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:74 — [P1/100] `const uniqueGuests = guests.filter(`: this check-then-insert neither deduplicates the request itself nor atomically excludes attendees added by a concurrent request, so duplicate attendee rows can be created (or the whole mutation can race into a constraint failure) without an idempotency mechanism.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P2/100] `guests: z.array(z.string().email()),`: the public mutation places no maximum on a caller-controlled collection that is materialized, inserted, translated, synchronized, and emailed in one request, creating an unbounded fan-out and resource-exhaustion cliff.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:168 — [P2/100] `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests);`: passing the raw requested list instead of the persisted `uniqueGuests` changes recipient semantics, so an already-existing attendee included alongside a genuinely new address is misclassified and sent a fresh scheduling email rather than the guest-change notification.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:1 — [P1/100] `# Task: Add guest management functionality to existing bookings`: the task defines no acceptance criteria or verification for authorization, eligible booking states, attendee persistence, calendar propagation, or notification behavior, so completion cannot be established against a reviewable contract.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:168 — [P1/100] `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests);`: when a request mixes a genuinely new address with an existing or blacklisted address, persistence filters the latter out but notification classification still treats it as newly added, sending an incorrect fresh-booking email to an address that was not added.

packages/emails/email-manager.ts:529 — [P1/75] `emailsToSend.push(sendEmail(() => new OrganizerAddGuestsEmail({ calEvent: calendarEvent })));`: the new notification flow unconditionally emails hosts and every attendee and omits the existing host/attendee disable-standard-email checks, leaving notification-preference behavior uncovered for this booking update.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:158 — [P1/100] `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);`: the handler explicitly permits any attendee at lines 52–56, but then attempts the organizer-owned calendar update with that attendee's credentials, so permitted attendee requests cannot reliably authenticate to or update the booking's calendar provider.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:54 — [P1/100] `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee)`: treating any attendee as authorized lets an invitee mutate the organizer's booking, add arbitrary recipients, and disclose the meeting invitation/details without organizer approval.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P1/100] `guests: z.array(z.string().email()),`: the server places no maximum on guest count, so any authorized attendee can amplify one request into unbounded database inserts, calendar updates, and outbound email fan-out for resource exhaustion and spam.

packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:77 — [P2/100] `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`: blacklist entries are lowercased but submitted addresses are not, so changing letter case bypasses the intended blocked-recipient security control.

goldens.comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:165 — [P1/100] `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);`: the database insert has already committed before this fallible external-calendar call, so a provider failure leaves durable attendees absent from the calendar and a retry rejects them as already present instead of repairing the partial state.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the code flow. Looking at addGuests.handler.ts, the database update (prisma.booking.update at line ~89-103) commits the new attendees to the database first, then later (line ~165) calls eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking) to sync with external calendars. If the calendar update fails, the attendees are already persisted in the database. On retry, the uniqueGuests filter (lines 69-73) would filter out these emails since they're now in booking.attendees, resulting in an 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' error. This is a legitimate atomicity/consistency issue where a partial failure leaves the system in an inconsistent state that cannot be easily repaired through retry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P2/100] `guests: z.array(z.string().email()),`: the public mutation places no maximum on a caller-controlled collection that is materialized, inserted, translated, synchronized, and emailed in one request, creating an unbounded fan-out and resource-exhaustion cliff.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security concern. Looking at the diff, the schema at addGuests.schema.ts defines `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no maximum length limit. In addGuests.handler.ts, this array is processed through multiple expensive operations: database inserts via `createMany`, translation lookups for each attendee, calendar synchronization via `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, and email sending via `sendAddGuestsEmails`. The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts creates email promises for each attendee. A malicious caller could submit thousands of email addresses in a single request, causing database bloat, excessive API calls to calendar providers, and mass email sending - all unbounded resource consumption. This is a legitimate denial-of-service vulnerability in a public mutation endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:168 — [P1/100] `await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests);`: when a request mixes a genuinely new address with an existing or blacklisted address, persistence filters the latter out but notification classification still treats it as newly added, sending an incorrect fresh-booking email to an address that was not added.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code flow: `uniqueGuests` filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails (line 68-72). Then `guestsFullDetails` is created from `uniqueGuests` (line 77). The database is updated with `guestsFullDetails` (line 85-97). However, at line 168, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original `guests` array, not `uniqueGuests`. Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails`, the logic checks `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` to decide whether to send `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (fresh booking email) or `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. Since `guests` contains the original unfiltered list including potentially existing/blacklisted emails, but those emails were filtered out and not added to the database, the `newGuests.includes()` check would return true for emails that weren't actually added. However, since those emails were filtered out and not added to `bookingAttendees.attendees`, they won't be in `calendarEvent.attendees` when iterating. So the issue is actually the opposite - the `guests` parameter might include emails that don't exist in `attendees`, so they won't receive any email. But the finding claims existing attendees would get wrong emails - this is incorrect because existing attendees ARE in the attendees list but their email is NOT in the original `guests` array (they were already there), so they'd correctly get `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. The real bug is that `guests` should be `uniqueGuests` for consistency, but the actual impact described in the finding is not accurate.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:158 — [P1/100] `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);`: the handler explicitly permits any attendee at lines 52–56, but then attempts the organizer-owned calendar update with that attendee's credentials, so permitted attendee requests cannot reliably authenticate to or update the booking's calendar provider.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in addGuests.handler.ts, the handler allows three types of users to add guests: team admin/owner, organizer, or attendee (lines 47-53). However, at line 158, it calls `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` which gets the credentials of the currently logged-in user (ctx.user), not the booking organizer. Then at line 160-163, it creates an EventManager with these credentials and calls `updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. If an attendee (who is not the organizer) calls this endpoint, they won't have the organizer's calendar credentials, so the calendar update would fail or use wrong credentials. This is a real authorization/functionality bug - attendees are permitted to add guests but the calendar update logic assumes organizer credentials.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts:54 — [P1/100] `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee)`: treating any attendee as authorized lets an invitee mutate the organizer's booking, add arbitrary recipients, and disclose the meeting invitation/details without organizer approval.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the authorization check at line 54 allows any attendee (isAttendee) to add guests to a booking. Looking at the code, isAttendee is determined by checking if the current user's email matches any attendee email in the booking. This means any guest who was invited to a meeting can add additional guests without the organizer's approval. This is a legitimate security/authorization concern - typically only organizers or team admins should be able to modify meeting attendees. The code explicitly allows attendees to add guests, which could lead to unauthorized disclosure of meeting details to arbitrary third parties and modification of the organizer's calendar events.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.schema.ts:5 — [P1/100] `guests: z.array(z.string().email()),`: the server places no maximum on guest count, so any authorized attendee can amplify one request into unbounded database inserts, calendar updates, and outbound email fan-out for resource exhaustion and spam.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the ZAddGuestsInputSchema in addGuests.schema.ts defines `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` without any maximum length constraint. Looking at the handler in addGuests.handler.ts, for each guest: 1) database inserts are created via `createMany`, 2) calendar updates are triggered via `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, and 3) emails are sent via `sendAddGuestsEmails`. The authorization check allows any attendee of the booking to add guests (line 47: `isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(...)`). This means any attendee could submit thousands of email addresses in a single request, causing unbounded database writes, calendar API calls, and email sends. This is a legitimate resource exhaustion and potential spam vector - a real security/DoS concern.
